title: Valuing a Stock
intro: Valuation turns a view about a company's future into a price you'd be willing to pay. The two main tools are multiples (what similar businesses sell for) and discounted cash flow (what the future cash is worth today). Neither gives the 'right' answer; both force you to make your assumptions explicit.

blocks.text: Price and value

Price is what you pay; value is what you get (Benjamin Graham's line, made famous by Buffett). The value of any asset is the present value of the cash it will produce for its owners. A stock price embeds the market's average forecast of that cash and its risk. To beat the market you need to be right where the market is wrong, which is hard because the market is the combined forecast of many well-informed people. Valuation is still worth doing even if you only buy index funds: it tells you whether expected returns are high or low.
Multiples

items: Price / earnings (P/E): price / EPS. A P/E of 20 means you pay \$20 for each \$1 of yearly earnings; its inverse, the earnings yield (5% here), is easy to compare with bond yields. Trailing P/E uses the last 12 months; forward P/E uses analysts' forecasts.
PEG ratio: P/E divided by the expected growth rate in percent. A PEG near 1 is a rough rule of fairness for growth companies.
Price / book (P/B): market cap / book equity. Useful for banks and insurers whose assets are mostly financial and marked near market value.
Price / sales (P/S): for companies with no profits yet; dangerous, because sales are not profits.

EV / EBITDA: enterprise value (market cap + debt − cash, plus preferred and minority interests) over EBITDA. Because EV includes debt it compares companies with different borrowing fairly, which P/E does not.
Dividend yield and free cash flow yield (FCF / market cap).

blocks.text: Multiples are quick and anchor you to the market, but they hide assumptions: a P/E is a compressed DCF. Compare only like with like (same industry, similar growth and risk), and remember that a sector can be expensive as a whole.
The Shiller CAPE

Robert Shiller's cyclically adjusted P/E (CAPE) divides the market's price by the average of ten years of inflation-adjusted earnings, smoothing out booms and recessions. Historically a high CAPE has been followed by lower ten-year returns, though with wide error bands and little use for timing next year. US CAPE has been well above its long-run average of about 17 for most of the past 30 years.
The dividend discount and Gordon growth models
If a stock's value is the present value of all its future dividends, and dividends grow forever at a constant rate $g$, the sum is a growing perpetuity (Myron Gordon, 1959):

blocks.caption: Gordon growth model: D_1 is next year's dividend, r the required return, g the growth rate.

blocks.text: A stock paying \$2.00 next year, growing 4% a year, with a required return of 8%, is worth $2 / (0.08 - 0.04) = \$50$. Rearranged, the model gives the market's implied return: $r = D_1/P_0 + g$, dividend yield plus growth, the same building blocks as on the Stocks page.

The model is extremely sensitive to $r - g$: at $r = 7\%$ the same stock is worth \$66.67, at 9% \$40. It needs $g < r$, and $g$ must be a rate the company can sustain forever, which means no faster than the economy's nominal growth (about 3 to 5%).
Since $D_1 = \text{EPS}_1 \times \text{payout}$, the model also explains a P/E: $P/E = \text{payout}/(r - g)$. Higher growth and lower risk justify a higher P/E.
Discounted cash flow (DCF)
A DCF values the whole business from its free cash flow, in two stages: an explicit forecast for 5 to 10 years, and a terminal value for everything after, usually by the Gordon formula:

items: Discount free cash flow to the firm (before interest) at the weighted average cost of capital (WACC) to get enterprise value; subtract net debt to get equity value; divide by shares for value per share.

$WACC = \frac{E}{D+E} r_E + \frac{D}{D+E} r_D (1 - t)$, where the cost of equity $r_E$ usually comes from CAPM (see Portfolio Theory) and the cost of debt $r_D$ from the company's bond yields; interest is tax-deductible, hence the $(1 - t)$.
Alternatively discount free cash flow to equity (after interest and debt flows) at the cost of equity to get equity value directly.

config.yLabel: value (same units as the cash flow)

blocks.text: Two lessons stand out from the plot. First, the terminal value is usually more than half, often three-quarters, of the total: most of a company's value lies beyond any forecast you can make with confidence. Second, a one-point change in the discount rate moves the value by roughly 10 to 20%. A DCF is a tool for asking 'what do I have to believe to justify this price?', not a machine for producing a precise number.
Reverse DCF

Instead of forecasting and computing a value, take today's price and solve for the growth rate it implies. If a stock only makes sense with 25% growth for ten years, you can ask how many companies have ever done that (very few). Michael Mauboussin and Alfred Rappaport's *Expectations Investing* is built on this idea.
Margin of safety and the quality of a business

Because every valuation is uncertain, Graham advised buying only well below your estimate of value, a margin of safety that absorbs mistakes. Later investors (Buffett, Munger, Fisher) added that the quality of the business matters as much as the price: a company with a durable competitive advantage (a moat, from brands, network effects, switching costs, scale or patents) can reinvest at a high ROIC for decades, and that compounding is worth paying for.

items: What does the company sell, to whom, and why do customers choose it?
What protects its profits from competitors, and is that protection growing or shrinking?
How much capital does growth need, and what return does that capital earn?
How is management paid, and how have they spent shareholders' money in the past?
What would have to happen for this investment to lose half its value?

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Gordon growth
blocks.text: A utility will pay a dividend of \$3.00 next year. You expect 3% growth forever and require 7%. What is it worth? What if growth is 4%?
solution: At 4%: $3.00 / 0.03 = \$100$. A one-point change in long-run growth changed the value by a third.

blocks.title: Implied return
blocks.text: An index fund yields 1.6% in dividends (on next year's dividend) and you expect its dividends to grow 5% a year over the long run. What return does the Gordon model imply?

blocks.title: Enterprise value
blocks.text: Company X has a market cap of \$8 billion, \$3 billion of debt and \$1 billion of cash; EBITDA is \$1.25 billion. Company Y has a market cap of \$9 billion, no debt, \$0.5 billion of cash and EBITDA of \$1.1 billion. Which is cheaper on EV/EBITDA?
solution: Y: $EV = 9 - 0.5 = 8.5$; $8.5 / 1.1 \approx 7.7\times$. Y is slightly cheaper, though X looks cheaper on market cap alone.

blocks.title: A small DCF
blocks.text: A business will produce free cash flow of \$100 next year, \$110 the year after and \$121 in year 3, then grow 3% a year forever. At a 9% discount rate, what is it worth?
solution: Total $\approx \$1{,}882$, of which the terminal value is 85%.

blocks.title: What the price assumes
blocks.text: A stock trades at \$100 and pays no dividend. Its free cash flow is \$2 a share this year. If you require 9% and expect FCF to grow at rate $g$ forever (so the next cash flow is $2(1 + g)$), what $g$ does the price imply?
solution: The market is pricing in about 6.9% growth forever, well above the economy's long-run nominal growth. That can be justified only by a period of much faster growth first, so the real question is how long and how fast.
